utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know exactly how the Chamber wishes to proceed this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it may be convenient if I summarise briefly the documents that we've had, and then we'll hear any submissions that you wish to make on the matter, and then we'll hear the government representatives. The order, as I said, was the 4th of February of this year for the production of documents within 60 days. We have received two reports on service by the Federation. Mr. Ahmic reported on the 6th of April that only the Minister of the Interior had communicated that it did not have any of the documents, the order having been forwarded to the appropriate ministries. Mr. Tomic reported on the 9th of April that he had received none of the documents. Those two gentlemen have been authorised to appear for the Federation. We have your application on the 16th of April, Mr. Nice, requesting a hearing for the representatives of the Federation to appear to explain why compliance cannot be expected or obtained or to show cause why the Trial Chamber should not find that the Federation is in breach of the order of the Trial Chamber. We, on the 27th of April, ordered that there should be a hearing today to allow the representatives of the Federation to explain why it hasn't complied with the previous order. While I'm dealing with these preliminary matters, I should say that such remedy as the Chamber may have, the Rule which applies to a hearing of this sort appears in Rule 7 bis(A), which provides that, "... where a Trial Chamber or a Judge is satisfied that a State has failed to comply with an obligation under Article 29 of the Statute which relates to any proceedings before that Chamber or Judge, the Chamber or Judge may advise the President, who shall report the matter to the Security Council." The other matter of law to which I would refer, to put this hearing into context, is the Blaskic appeal decision of the 29th of October of 1997, which dealt with these matters. At paragraph 35 of the judgment, the Appeal Chamber said that, "When faced with an allegation of non-compliance with an order or request issued under Article 29, a Trial Chamber must be satisfied that the State has clearly failed to comply with the order or request." They went on to point out that, "This finding is totally different from that made at the request of the Security Council by a fact-finding body and, a fortiori, from that undertaken by a political or quasi-political body. Depending upon the circumstances, the determination by the latter may undoubtedly constitute an authoritative statement of what has occurred in a particular area of interest to the Security Council." Then going on to the end of the paragraph, "By contrast, the International Tribunal, i.e., a Trial Chamber, a Judge, or the President, engages in a judicial activity proper, acting upon all the principles and rules of judicial propriety, it scrutinises the behaviour of a certain State in order to establish formally whether or not that State has breached its international obligation to cooperate with the International Tribunal." Mr. Nice, I refer to those matters because it's against that background or within that framework that the Trial Chamber must conduct the hearing and make any finding. Now, is there anything you want to add? You've made your request.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've made our request. There are, I think, a few things that I should say at this stage to put things in context. First, so far as remedies are concerned, of course, if the Chamber is able to pursue the matter today by obtaining from either representative the identification of someone who presently knows or, indeed, at any time has known, I dare say, the whereabouts of the material that is sought, then steps may be taken in respect of a named individual, which could ultimately lead to the provisions of Rule 77 becoming appropriate if compliance isn't made; that is to say, contempt. We would ask you to have in mind, in relation to this matter, the pursuit of named individuals who can help you further. Today's hearing comes at the end of a long history, but Your Honour has encapsulated what is material for today's hearing, although it may be helpful for the Chamber generally if I say just the following: First, as the Chamber knows and as is set out in our application, the Federation is represented by two individuals because, in large measure, there are two separate systems in operation there which are by no means necessarily in harmony. Again, as I think the Chamber will know from its experience generally, the Chamber and the Office of the Prosecutor has always enjoyed very considerable cooperation with and from the Bosniak side, represented today by Mr. Ahmic, and the Chamber will see that his explanation is full and it's not one which we in any way challenge. The same cannot be said of the other part of the Federation, represented by Mr. Tomic. Second, there is no challenge so far before you to the suggestion that these documents have existed, or indeed still exist. Again, the Chamber, from its dealings with this case, and generally, may know and accept that a tradition of documentation that existed before 1990 persisted after the changes in the former Yugoslavia, and as I say but repeat, there is no evidence nor suggestion that the documents identified either don't exist or have been destroyed. Third, as the Chamber may know from elsewhere, but it's important that I should tell you in case you don't, in his evidence in the Blaskic case, the defendant, Blaskic, himself made it clear that there existed as late as the autumn of 1995 a complete war archive, for he spoke, I think, in giving evidence, from notes which he asserted he had compiled from that very war archive which he had been able fully to research. I believe, indeed, the Blaskic Trial Chamber has made an order in respect of the original material consequent on his evidence, but what is clear, and no doubt would not be denied by Mr. Tomic, is that that war archive existed in 1995. There are, therefore, people within the Federation -- and it will be the Croat side of the Federation -- who knew then and who know now what has happened to that archive. I can tell Your Honour this, that the location spoken of by Blaskic in his own defence as the place where the archive was to be found is not one that has been visited for search by the Office of the Prosecutor and wasn't covered on an earlier occasion by such process. Mr. Scott has prepared a most helpful and full chronology of events. I'm afraid that it's at the moment only in English, and I apologise for that, but it wasn't realised how substantial it would be until it was very recently looked into. I can make that available to you now, or possibly later, depending on whether you would prefer to hear straightaway an explanation from the representatives of the Federation; but it's our submission to you that the answers that have been thus far provided in the reports, and in the very short report of Mr. Tomic, leave unanswered questions that the Chamber would itself want to have answered. These documents are, of course, of absolutely fundamental importance to the work of this Chamber. If they were produced, and if, as there's no reason to doubt, they would provide a full working record of what happened, then nearly all, if not all, the issues that are having to be litigated second-hand, or indeed litigated in some instances by the process of inference, would be established directly by contemporaneous material, material that for example apparently includes a report prepared contemporaneously, on the orders of Blaskic, about the massacre at Ahmici, but I cite that as but one example. So these documents would make your task infinitely easier, would indeed save an enormous amount of time, and there can only be one reason why those documents are being kept from you, by whatever process; hiding, dispersion, possibly destruction, removal to another State. There can only be one reason, and that is because they would be revealing in a way that the custodians do not wish to allow. It may be helpful -- because I know people jumping up and sitting down again is unappealing -- it may be helpful if I have distributed at this stage the chronology and perhaps ask Mr. Scott to take you through it very, very quickly. Would that be helpful?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If that can be distributed as well to Mr. Ahmic and Mr. Tomic, and I'll ask Mr. Scott to deal with it as briefly as he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the usher could also provide to the Court simultaneously, please, a packet of materials, the first one of which is a subpoena duces tecum from Judge McDonald, and the two separate things can be used to some extent side by side.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have copies, too, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The interpreters have asked for copies as well, if we have enough. I hope we do. As the Court is beginning to know by now, I suppose, in seeing me stand up in court, I find written outlines and notes to be certainly helpful for me, and I hope for the Court as well, in moving through what is often otherwise lengthy and complex material. The Court will now have this and can certainly peruse it both this morning and at other times when it sees fit. As Mr. Nice said, I don't intend go through it word by word by any means, but I do believe the Court will find it most instructive in the issues before the Court. What the Court will note immediately is that -- in many ways unfortunately -- we come here today as part of a story that started almost two and a half years ago when a subpoena was issued by Judge McDonald, which is the first document in the separate stack of documents that has been distributed, which, when the Court has the opportunity to review in full, the Court will see that many of the same documents and much of the same information that we are asking for today, or asked for in February of this year, has been asked for and sought after since January of 1997. And I will represent to the Court that in large measure, in substantially a majority -- in substantially major measure, to this day, those documents and materials have not been provided to the Tribunal, either in the Blaskic case or now in the Kordic case. With that in mind, we start with, simply, in item 1 on the chronology, Your Honours, the fact that it's beyond dispute, I believe, that an archive was set up by the legislation of what was then the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, in March of 1993, coming from what's referenced here as the Official Gazette, or the Court may have heard by now or will hear in the future, the Narodni List. The Court will then note that as it relates to some of the specific events in this case -- and this chronology is rather a unified document which essentially ties a number of different events and issues into one single document, because the Ahmici issue will come up both momentarily and later, in the new application that will be reviewed later. On the 16th of April, as the Court well knows by now, is the attack on Ahmici. On the 10th of May, then-Colonel Blaskic orders an investigation into Ahmici. On the 25th of May, Mr. Sliskovic, who was the intelligence officer, assistant chief for Central Bosnia for essentially intelligence in the secret police or the SIS, provided a very -- what you might call preliminary report; and I note here, Your Honour, that despite repeated efforts by this Court, by other Trial Chambers, and certainly by the Prosecutor, to date, this report -- which, as Mr. Nice has indicated, could conceivably be one of the most important documents that any of us could ever see on these issues -- has never been provided, even in Colonel Blaskic's own testimony in his own defence in the Blaskic case, he himself has confirmed that these reports existed, that he ordered it, that he saw them at one point, and that he saw them at least in part in 1995 when he himself visited the archive. You will see -- I'm going to jump through the next series of events -- you will see them. They are largely self-explanatory. There is a further subpoena -- well, this is the subpoena we were just referring to, the next-to-last item on page 2, by Judge McDonald to the Federation, the very Federation that appears before the Court this morning, and to the custodian of the records of the central archive, et cetera. At that very point in time, the prime minister, the prime minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina, directed the federal defence minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina to comply, a senior member of the Federation government, at that time was Mr. Ante Jelavic. Going to the top of the next page, page 3 of the summary, on February the 21st of 1997, the prime minister again directed Mr. Jelavic to comply, in very specific terms, which I again will not read to the Court, but the excerpt is there. Some of these documents, Your Honour, but only a sampling, are in the packet of materials that I've provided to the Court. Again, the Court will quickly note there are more entries on this document, on the summary, than there are documents in this packet, so I will tell the Court this is simply, if you will, a sampling. We are certainly happy to provide the Court with any document that the Court would like that's listed or referenced in this summary. There then comes a series of orders and additional subpoenas, the Court will see, from Judge McDonald in the early part of 1997. Mr. Jelavic, in late February and early March of 1997, actually ordered all HVO commanders -- I'm looking at about the fifth item on page 3 -- "Orders all HVO commanders to gather and catalogue all available archives." "Orders all HVO commanders to protect against damage, destruction, removal and relocation all archives subject to the above order." What is interesting about that, one of the things that's interesting about those orders, is that the Court will then jump one item down to the 14th of March 1997, there is then a letter addressed to this Court in which the same Mr. Jelavic takes the position, quotes, in an official representation to this Court, that, "According to the information at my disposal the Croatian Defence Council" -- that is, the HVO -- "as an army formed during the war, never had a centralised military archive." And what we hope the Court will ultimately conclude and the evidence will show and what this submission shows, Your Honour, is that that is simply -- let me say untrue. Whether it was an intentional lie, we can all draw our own conclusions ultimately. It was clearly untrue. There is then a series of additional exchanges, about the fourth item on page 4 at one point Mr. Jelavic appears to suggest that while he doesn't have jurisdiction over the archives that it really should be the Minister of Justice and there is a letter then from the Minister of Justice Mato Tadic who says, "We [The Federal Ministry of Justice] have no jurisdiction over the war archive, but it falls within the competence of the Ministry of Defence." There are then additional subpoenas and orders from Judge McDonald. There is also on the next item for the 18th of June, 1997, the Prosecutor's report which essentially, if you will Your Honour, summarises the history up to that point in time which can do, and probably does, it more effectively and more efficiently than I would do if we went through it in detail this morning. I have a copy of that Your Honour, and I didn't give it to the usher before because it is a confidential, under-seal document, and for that reason if I tender it to the Court subject to the Court's direction. I'm not providing it to the representatives of the Federation. So if I could hand that to the usher, again, solely for the Court and its staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is there some matter you want us to rely on in that letter, before it's handed to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you will see, when you have a chance to look at it, that what the Prosecutor did in this document is go through in more detail than I have in the last ten minutes the entire history and all the steps to obtain compliance. The Court can simply take it as historical statement, if you will, which I could simply go into in the same fashion, if time allowed. But when the Court has a chance to look at the document I think it will speak for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We must finish this hearing by half past 12 and that includes, Mr. Scott, the second application.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to jump dramatically now and only head on to the bottom of page 5, I'm only going to say this is for the entry of the 12th of March, 1999, this year. This is what then Colonel Blaskic said himself about Ahmici, that it was an organised criminal act, et cetera, et cetera. And again that is the reason why he asked for himself, on at least two occasions, for an investigation to be completed by his own essentially military police or intelligence investigative service. The Court will find Mr. Blaskic's own testimony, I think, insightful. Then, here is also directing to the bottom of page 6, Your Honour, this is what, as Mr. Nice referred to earlier, this is what Mr. Blaskic has testified to as recently as a few weeks ago under oath in his own case about the archive, the very archive, about the very documents that we were seeking and that the Prosecutor has been seeking since January of 1997. Blaskic says, I went there in November of 1995, it was there, it was in a town called Siroki Brijeg, he went through voluminous documents et cetera, and again, in interests of time I wouldn't go through it, but the Court will see the documents very clearly; logbooks, orders, military diaries, all were there and were all seen and used by Colonel Blaskic in preparing his defence. Because of that -- I'm skipping now, Your Honour, all the way to page 9 -- because of that, on the 22nd of April, just a few weeks ago, the Blaskic Trial Chamber ordered both the Defence in that case and this same Federation to produce the materials relied upon, and I've excerpted parts of the order here, which I'll just briefly mention, which just simply says, "Considering that the accused," Blaskic, "who is appearing as a witness ... stated that, in order to prepare his defence in the present case he relied on the personal notes he drafted ..." et cetera, et cetera, during a visit to the archives of his headquarters. The Court directed, "all right, let's see these materials. You've relied on them extensively in your Defence, let us all have access to the same materials." The Court directed that those materials be provided to the Prosecutor and to the Tribunal by the 15th of May, which was last Saturday. It is directly related to much of the same material and information that we seek, Your Honours. So not only -- I think it's fair to observe in this context -- not only are we here today on the non-compliance by the Federation of your order on the 4th of February of this year but now the failure to comply with the Blaskic order, which is also outstanding, for essentially many of the same materials. They are twice in violation. Your Honour, that is where we are. We believe that these documents have existed, either still exist, or the Court is deserves to be told what happened to them. And I'll stop there for the time being, subject to the Court's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, if you turn back to page 3 of your very helpful summary, at the bottom, I'm referring to the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: From the Minister of Defence denying that the Croatian Defence Council as an army formed during the war ever had a centralised military archive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That letter, I'm not sure whether we have it here, but are you able to say whether there was anything else in that letter which was advanced to substantiate the denial?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there is -- you do have the letter, it is in the packet of documents which are pretty much in chronological order, Your Honours, and without a page reference, I apologise, I can only say that it's approximately halfway through the stack. It is dated the 14th of March, 1997, in another notation up in the upper right corner, someone has written "575" or "573 A". Mr. Jelavic does go on, after the quoted statement in the second paragraph, to provide some additional information. I will tell the Court again, skipping over the outline to some extent, Mr. Jelavic, by the end of 1997, took the position with the Prosecutor and the Court that there had been compliance at least by that late -- well, at that time late date, but I can tell the Court, in anticipating possible questions from the Court, the Prosecutor to this date, and I've spoken with Mr. Harmon on this as well, considers that production at the end of 1997 to be grossly deficient. There were a few documents that were handed over that were non-responsive. I hope that's helpful to Judge Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will turn to the representatives of the Federation, and it may be convenient to hear from Mr. Ahmic first.

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have your letter of the 6th of April in which you say that the order was communicated by yourself in February to the Prime Minister and, in turn, was forwarded to the Ministry of Defence, the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of Interior, with the request to undertake all activities in their competence as to comply with the order. But so far, only the Ministry of Interior, as I said, had communicated that the information requested was not in their possession. What would you like to say to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, Your Honours. I submitted the report to the Court on the 7th of April, 1992, in which I reported what the ministries in question had done, that is, the ministries making part of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that was the report that you had just read. I should like to complement it with the report of the Prime Minister, if I may, which we received on the 17th of May, '99, and where we see a brief overview of what Mr. Edhem Bicakcic, that is, the Prime Minister of the Federation, did with regard to the order of this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think we've seen a copy of that report. Has it been forwarded to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) No, the Tribunal has not received this letter because I received it yesterday. It was written on the 17th, I received it only yesterday, and I have here the copies of the report with all the annexes. If I may, I should like to distribute it now, and I have copies for Your Honours and for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I should merely like to add that there is also a drafted translation into English of the report and all the documents attached to it, but it is an unofficial translation. There are two copies, one for the Court and one for the Prosecution. If I may, I should like to read this report in total. It is not long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We now have the copy in front of us. At least I have a copy. My colleagues do not. Therefore, it may be best if you would summarise for us the contents, because that makes for easier translation. The one copy can go on the ELMO, and I'm going to put on the English translation, and then if it's on the ELMO, you could perhaps read it out, Mr. Ahmic.

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. If you would like to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. The title of the document is "The International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia, Trial Chamber III." It is on the 17th of May, 1999, number O1-2-318/99-3. "The Federal Prime Minister reports that the order of the Trial Chamber of the ICTY for the production of documents issued on the 4th of February, 1999, and communicated to the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Bosnia-Herzegovina was received on the 8th of February, 1999. "On the 9th of February, 1999, by letter number 01-02-318/99 of the Prime Minister of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Federation, the order was passed to the Federal Defence Ministry to the attention of the ministry, Mr. Miroslav Prce ..." And I need to mention that he is a representative of the Croats people and is a high official in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, representing the Croat people. "... then to the Federal Ministry of Justice, to the attention of minister Ignjacije Dodik ..." and this is an official representing the Bosniak people in the authorities of the Bosnian Croat Federation. As the Court is well aware of, these ministers should undertake all the activities, in compliance with their competence, so as to execute the order of the ICTY Trial Chamber within the said period of time. Attention was also drawn by the Federal Prime Minister to the fact that the [indiscernible] of the order was of a confidential nature, that its publication was not allowed. Furthermore, prior to the expiration of the said deadline of 60 days for the production of the requested documents, by the letter of the 4th of April, 1999, the Federal Prime Minister, in his letter 01-02-0308/99, requesting relevant ministries once again to actually provide the feedback about the measures taken, and this letter is enclosed herewith. I'm reading the document sent by the Federal Ministry of the Interior on the 7th of March, '99. Its number is strictly [indiscernible] with actual number 10-03-25/1, and the Federal Minister of Information informs that it, I'm quoting, it did not have the documents listed in the confidential annex to the order available. The order was then passed on to the Federal army, the section of security and intelligence, to the Deputy Federal Minister of the Interior representing the Croat people in the Federal Ministry of the Interior, ministers of the Interior of the Central Bosnian canton, and of the Herzegovina Neretva canton. The former has its seat in Travnik and the latter in Mostar, and they were requested to act under the order within the said period of time. In this letter of the Federal Ministry of the Interior, it is said that the section of security and intelligence of the Federal Ministry of Defence has informed them that the documents listed in the confidential annex of the order relate entirely to the HVO component of the army of the Federation. Furthermore, after the expiration of the 60-day time limit as envisaged by the order of this Trial Chamber, the Federal Defence minister, Miroslav Prce, representing the Croat people on the authorities of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, also issued a document on the 19th of April, number 01-03-2-1/99, and in this document, he wrote as follows, I'm quoting, "In respect of the order for the production of documents addressed to the BH Federation and issued by the Trial Chamber of the ICTY in the case 'Prosecutor v. Mario Cerkez and Dario Kordic,' we would like to advise you that the Federal Ministry of Defence does not have any archive material dating from the period in respect of which the documents are sought available, and, therefore, we would like to direct you to turn to relevant institutions in charge of the custody of archival material since we do not know whether they are in possession of any of the requested documents." We therefore sent the above-mentioned letter of the Federal Ministry of Defence, Mr. Prce. A reply was requested by the Prime Minister, Edhem Bicakcic, requested a reply from the archive of the BH Federation. The answer of the archive came on the 11th of May, 1999, and under the number 01-1-05-1/1-99, and there the archive of the BH Federation, in its letter, explicitly states the following, and I quote. "... the archive of the BH Federation has, ever since it began its work on the 1st of June, 1997, has not taken over a single holding from any of the authorities or any other institution organised at the level of the BH Federation." At the end of this report, the Federal Minister of Justice, Mr. Ignjacije Dodik, an official representing the Croat people in the authorities of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Prime Minister says that he has not been informed by the Federal Minister of Justice about these measures at all. In the end, I should like to add that yesterday, on the 19th of May, the Federal Prime Minister, Mr. Bicakcic, sent me a letter which I received yesterday, in which the Federal Ministry of Justice informs the Federal Prime Minister that the Federal Ministry of Justice was approached by Miroslav Prce, the Federal Defence minister, and with the letter of the 10th of May, 1999, number 06-03-297/99, and in this letter the Federal Defence minister, Mr. Prce, informs, and I quote, "In May, 1992, there did not exist Federal institutions and instead there were only mono-ethnic institutions in operation. We are not legal successors to those, and their documentation has not been placed at our disposal. We therefore wish to inform you that we are not in a position to extend to you the assistance as required, and we suggest that you approach the successors to the above-mentioned authorities."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, what you've just quoted was a reply from which ministry, Justice or Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The Federal Defence ministry, Mr. Prce, and through the Ministry of Justice, he sent the letter to the Federal Prime Minister. Yes, it is a little bit complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So I expect you're coming to deal with the question of a reply from the Ministry of Justice itself, because so far, from what I have gathered, there's no reply from the Ministry of Justice, which was written to by the Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, that is true, that is so. You are quite right, Your Honour. That is why the Federal Prime Minister also shows, in his report, that within those 60 days' time limit and even after the expiration of that, he has received absolutely no report from the Federal Ministry of Justice. I should like to conclude that this report, as one authorised with the Federation, that this report and the former reports make it clear that within 60 days, the relevant ministers, Mr. Ignjacije Dodik and Mr. Miroslav Prce, who are officials representing the Croat people in the authorities of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Can we have the letter we just read from the Minister of Defence to the Minister of Justice on the ELMO, if you have it, the last letter we just read?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The 19th of May, the letter from the Prime Minister. Do we have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: From the Minister of Defence to the Minister of Justice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I temporarily withdraw?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll be back as soon as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, let us see if we can get this right. There is a letter written by the Prime Minister to you, is this right, of the 19th of May, and in that letter he refers to the reply, as I understood it, from the Ministry of Defence to him; is that right? You've never heard anything from the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Quite. Mr. Miroslav Prce, Minister of Defence, sent a letter which I do not have to the Minister of Justice, Mr. Ignjacije Dodik, and Mr. Dodik, as the Minister of Justice, then transmitted this letter to the Federal Prime Minister. That is, the Minister of Defence did not approach directly the Federal Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Can I have the letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: I don't think you have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, did you hand in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: He just read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Did you hand in the letter of the 19th of May which you just read out? Did you hand that in to the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps the Registrar could give back to Mr. Ahmic the documents and see if we can find it and put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, it is not included in this file, but I do have a copy myself. I have the letter here and a translation of the same letter into English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we got the letter now on the ELMO, please? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, I don't know if you are in a position now to answer to some complementary information about the content of this letter, because here in this letter the Minister of Defence is saying that, "We would like to inform you, in May, 1992, the federal institution had not existed. That means, rather, there were only uni-ethnic institutions." Can you give the Chamber some position about what is called here "uni-ethnic institution" first? That is my first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) That is the position of Mr. Prce, which certainly could be subject to a legal analysis. But in this position of his, I think that Mr. Prce is not right. At this point in time, I do not have the legal regulations with the help of which I could explain to Your Honours the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina in May, 1992, but all I can say, that this was a period when the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a state, existed, and I don't know what Mr. Prce is referring to when he talks about mono-ethnic institutions. But I can, I think, subsequently report to Your Honours the legal regulations in force in 1992 and how legal relations within the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina were regulated at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: I think it can be helpful to the Chamber. The second question. This letter, we can read the significant information here. "We are not the legal successors," so we are familiar with this problem of succession of states or governments of states here, "and therefore the document has not been put at our disposal. Hence, we would like to inform you that we are not in a position to offer you the appropriate assistance. However, we suggest that you address the successors of the mentioned institutions." Are you in a position to give to the Chamber some complementary information about who are now the successors, because we are advised to address to the successors of these institutions. Are you in a position to inform us who are the successors to the so-called uni-ethnic institutions or former institutions?

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I have to say again that I don't know what Mr. Prce meant when he mentions mono-ethnic institutions. All I know is that in May, '92, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina existed, as well as all its institutions, ranging from the presidency, the government, the parliament, et cetera. I don't know which mono-ethnic institutions Mr. Prce had in mind in this letter; probably institutions that only he is aware of. As for the second paragraph, may I ask Your Honours to look back at the report of the Federal Prime Minister, because I think the Federal Prime Minister, having received Mr. Price’s two letters, probably didn't understand which legal successors Mr. Prce had in mind, because he did not indicate who those successors, legal successors, are. That is why we can see, from the letter of the Prime Minister, that he addressed himself to the federal archive, that is, the archive of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, from which he received a reply saying that the federal archive had not succeeded any documents, as it was constituted only on the 1st of June, 1997, I think, and that it did not get hold of any holdings from the archive. May I also, as a third point, give explanations as to the possibility of who the legal successors may be? And I should like to refer you again to the statement by the learned counsel of the Prosecution, Mr. Scott. And during the hearing, I circled a document referred to by Mr. Scott in his presentation, in the summary. It is on page 4. The number of the document is 03/06/97. It is the letter of the Minister of Justice, Mr. Mato Tadic -- and may I add that Mr. Tadic is a representative of the Croatian people in those days, in the bodies and institutions of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that Mr. Mato Tadic, as a representative of the Croatian people, reported that the Federal Ministry of Justice, if I am translating this well from the English, has no jurisdiction over the war archive, but that the archive falls within the competence of the federal Ministry of Defence. If I have been of any assistance to Your Honours, Mr. Prce said something that in my view simply doesn't stand, is not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Does that mean that the war archive, according to this letter of 3 June '97, is under the authority of the Ministry of Defence? That means that the war archive now, in the Croatian part, perhaps, of the Federation, is under the authority of the Minister of Defence? Can you confirm that, Mr. Ahmic?

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I can just confirm, Your Honour, what is stated in his letter by Mr. Mato Tadic. And I think that in the Blaskic case, the subpoenas were in fact addressed to the then-minister of Defence, Mr. Anto Jelavic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, I have to say frankly, one of the matters that the Chamber has to decide on the basis of the Prosecutor's motion is whether the Federation is in breach of the order of this Chamber. The Chamber (sic) has an international obligation, and I want to stress that, an international obligation to comply with the order. In deciding whether the Federation has complied with the order, whether the Federation is in breach of the order, one of the matters that the Chamber has to take into account is the extent to which the Federation has acted in good faith. That is exceedingly important in this matter, the bona fides of the Federation, and I have to say very frankly that looking at this matter on the basis of the replies that have been given, I'm very doubtful as to whether I personally could conclude that the Federation has shown good faith in this matter. It is not good enough to come to this Chamber and say, as a representative of the Federation, that you do not know where the documents are. I have formed a view that these documents are in your country, and your country has a responsibility to disclose them on the basis of the order made by this Court. The discharge of your obligation, international obligation, is totally independent of the domestic constitutional structure of your country. Whether you have complied with the order or not does not depend on your internal structure. You have an international obligation, and you must comply with it. It is not for this Chamber to be going from one document to another document, seeing whether it's the Ministry of Defence or the Ministry of Justice. If there is a successor agency to the agency that existed before, then your obligation is to find that successor agency and get the information from them. If the information is not with the successor agency, then presumably it is somewhere else, and it is equally your obligation to get the information to the Court. It is not good enough to merely produce a letter from the prime minister saying that he has written to A, B, and C; C, in this case, is the Ministry of Justice, which has not even replied. It is the obligation of the prime minister, if he is acting in good faith, to secure a reply from the Ministry of Justice. You have pointed us to the letter of the 3rd of June '97 from the Minister of Justice, Mato Tadic. Presumably his response today would be the same as it was then, but it is very indicative of the efforts that your country has made that you have come to the Chamber today with no reply from the Minister of Justice to the prime minister's letter, regardless of what that reply would be. So I'm beginning to be very doubtful as to whether I could say, speaking for myself, that the Federation has acted in good faith in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I fully agree with Your Honour, Judge Robinson, that on the basis of these reports which I have conveyed to you as one of the representatives of the Federation -- and I beg you not to forget that we have a second representative of the Federation, Mr. Tomic, and I think he has great deal to say about the legal successors of the archive and the documentations. I think he could have a great deal to say as to what he has undertaken to comply with the order, because these are documents which clearly were created within the framework of the HVO, and Mr. Tomic, I think, is better informed than me because Mr. Tomic participated in the HVO structures, and I think he can be of considerable assistance. As far as I know, I think he was a secretary of the Croatian Defence Council of Herceg-Bosna in Mostar; he was an editor of the gazette, official gazette of Herceg-Bosna --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you, Mr. Ahmic, because Mr. Tomic can speak for himself; but what we would like is an answer to the point made by Judge Robinson. The point is this: That at the moment, on the documents which are put before us, it is the Federation which is in breach of its duty to comply with the order of the Court. The order was sent to the Federation, and the response that we get is that it is the responsibility, if anybody's, of a particular ministry. Now, we want to hear from Mr. Tomic. I would be grateful if, very briefly, you would tell us why you say it's not the fault of the Federation -- unless you accept the point that Judge Robinson made, that it is the fault of the Federation.

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I agree, Your Honour, but Your Honours, you have to bear in mind that the Federation and the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina were regulated by the Washington and Dayton agreements, and it is specific and unique in relation to all other states. When I say that the Federation has fulfilled its obligation, I'm referring to the component of the Federation consisting of the Bosniaks. In this case, I must say, unfortunately -- I do not like to speak about the ethnic origins of various people, but the constitution of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina has been conceived in such a way that ethnic parity representation is required in all the institutions of the Federation, and this is stated in the constitution. That means that the ethnic groups have to be equally represented in the organs of the Federation throughout. When I said that the Federation had complied, I was referring to the Bosniak component, the federal prime minister, Mr. Bicakcic, as the Bosniak representative, as the prime minister, has taken everything in his power to gain possession of the documents contained in the order of this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will hear now from Mr. Tomic. Mr. Tomic, what he has said is that this is the responsibility of the federal Minister of Defence or the federal Minister of Justice, those ministries, as I understand it, being part of the Croatian component in the Federation. Perhaps you could deal with those matters, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tomic. I'm sorry you were interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, Your Honours, as you have seen from my brief report, I informed the competent officials of the Federation about the order for the production of documents. Also, during my recent stay in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I personally informed the president of the Federation, Mr. Ivo Andric Luzanski, of the request of the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution. It is a fact that to date I have not received a single one of the requested documents. A detailed analysis of various jurisdictions that colleague Ahmic has referred to is something that I have little to add to without additional consultation with the appropriate ministers, either of Justice or of Defence. It is my opinion that it would be useful, in the interest of having full insight into the situation, to highlight a few points. It is a fact that a classical archive, an archive in the traditional sense, such as exists in modern countries, does not exist at this point in time in Bosnia-Herzegovina, at least as far as the component comprising the HVO is concerned. Due to wartime conditions -- I'm implying the purely technical aspect of the matter -- it would be difficult to find a particular document applying regular archival methods. This is point 1. The second point is that a large amount of archive documents disappeared. Some of them never even existed. Another part of the documentation was seized by the SFOR operation in the summer of last year. I shall take the liberty to express a personal opinion, and that is that I believe that a part of the documentation may have been in the possession of persons who played a certain role during the war and later died. It is also a fact that there was no strict control, nor was there a high level of archival ethics regarding the preservation of documents, and this is also evidenced by the fact that individual persons wrote their memoirs while the war was still going on, and this is something that cannot be done without a certain amount of documentation, and which could not have been taken away had a proper system been functioning in the archive. May I also recall the fact that U.S. General Bradley wrote his memoirs only in 1952 or 1953, in which he expressed his gratitude to the United States government for granting him permission to be able to write those memoirs. The same general states that the most important decisions of the Second World War were made without any written record being taken of them. So not a single army, and therefore the HVO as well, is a kind of insurance company that issues its decisions in two copies. Regarding the actual request of the Prosecution and the arguments provided in support of it, may I be allowed to say the following: The request does not fully correspond to the Appeals Chamber decision of the 27th of October, 1997, in the Blaskic case. The very wording saying that, quote, "all," end quote, letters, documents, records, video recordings, et cetera, are requested, does not facilitate compliance with such a request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Tomic, I don't think it's appropriate to challenge the order now. The order has been made. Now, as I understand the position which you're adopting, you're saying that you haven't got any documents anyway, and that there is no archive. If you're saying there may be documents but the order is not specific enough to identify them, why, then we will hear you on that point, as it may be possible that some of the documents could then be found. So are you saying that there may be some documents but you're not sure what they might be?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, Your Honour. Some documents may indeed exist somewhere, but I cannot really claim it with any amount of certainty at the present moment, and I likewise believe, Your Honour, that the manner in which the request was worded, I think, does give us the right to say what we think about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can't complain about the order, but if you say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) No, no, I'm not complaining; I'm not complaining. I am not questioning the right of the Prosecution to request whatever kind of documentation they like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, the point I'm making is this: If you say that you could identify the documents in some way if the order was rephrased or something of that sort, if that is what you're saying, how is it that the order should be rephrased to enable you to identify the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Let me quote a very simple example. It is not -- the time or the subject of any individual document are not indicated. It is quite possible that the Prosecution is asking for a series of documents which have become irrelevant in the meantime. The Prosecution's request -- and I really do not want to go into it; I shall try to write a brief in order to explain our view on the matter -- but the Prosecution's request is derived from a specific concept which again comes from certain views taken in advance. If it says, well, the head of state of one State has issued to a citizen of another State --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, we are not going to hear argument about the order. I thought that what you were saying was that some of these documents may exist but the order was too vague, or something of the sort, for you to identify it. But that is apparently not what you're saying. Now, apart from complaint about the order, have you got any other points you want to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, to put it mildly, this order is rather unique, and there is a tone in it which I find unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Look, Mr. Tomic, it's not for you to complain about the order, and I have said that more than once, and certainly it's not for you to complain about the tone of it. The order was made by this Trial Chamber, and you can't go back on it or go behind it. Now, if you've got nothing else to add, we're going to take the break, unless my colleagues have questions, which of course they can ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Tomic, I'll speak French this time. A question was asked a moment ago about the archives, about the existence of war archives which would exist at present: Do you know about them, do you have any knowledge about them, and whether they are in the HVO. In view of your position on the opposed, could you now answer us whether there are any wartime or military archives still in existence, whether there are these war archives, and whether they belong to the HVO. This is one question, and certainly whether they are held by the HVO; and secondly, is this under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Defence of the Federation, Mr. Prce? So will you please try to answer these two questions as briefly as possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, your question had also an introduction as regards my role in the HVO. Then I need to tell you that I have no role in the HVO, and this has been the case for a long time, even though I'm proud to say that I joined the HVO as a volunteer, with a rifle in my hands, at the time when many people who at present swear by the BH were on the run, and allied themselves with those who were attacking the BH at the time. So I do not have any role in the HVO. Without additional consultation, without seeking additional advice, I could not really tell you what is the exact situation with the archives at present. But since you called me out, and since I am being mentioned in this summary, I was absent for a while of late, because a few months ago, I submitted a request to the Court identifying some problems and some deviations, as I see them, for which this Trial Chamber now has difficulties in its work. From simple terminological matters, I'm very grateful to Mr. Ahmic for making it clear that Mr. Bicakcic is the Prime Minister of the Federation of BH, whereas this summary talks about the Prime Minister of BH, and that is the same difference as between the Prime Minister of Scotland and the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. For several years, this Tribunal -- I have not been able to prove some elementary things in this Tribunal: That there is no such thing as the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that the request of the Prosecution is based on some fictitious ideas. Of course I cannot prove it all. I can't. What I cannot prove to this Chamber -- that is, to another Chamber, not to you, but you are bearing the consequences of it -- I cannot, because nobody ever wanted to answer my motions. I requested an investigation into the work of the Court, or rather the Prosecution, and I believe that any investigation would result in the resignation of a number of persons in this Tribunal. Nobody has answered this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, you are here to give us an explanation about specific matters, not to make a speech, if I may say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I am really sorry that you failed to respond, Mr. Tomic. I am really sorry that you failed to answer my question; that is, you evaded the answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: (Microphone not activated)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Mr. Tomic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, Your Honours, I am not hesitating to answer, and please do not understand this as a lack of respect that I have for the Judges or for the Prosecution. With a situation which is not an ordinary situation, which is very complex, there are certain relations between the partners -- that is, between the Bosniaks and the Croats in the Federation -- and their relations are still very complicated. The premise of your question is that Bosnia-Herzegovina is a conventional state, a normal state. But (Latin phrase), that is, law derives from facts, on the fact that there is still a Bosnia-Herzegovina, but we have a different high -- we have a high commissioner, so we are not dealing here with a conventional case, as with, shall I say, a country like the United Kingdom or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Tomic, do not insist, really. We do have information, we're quite knowledgeable, we're quite conversant with the case in point. Perhaps you need some additional consultation, but I have not received from you the information that I sought. If you do conduct your consultations, you can still supply us with the information, but please, no speeches. We indeed do know quite a great deal about this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now for a quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I'm going to invite you to make some submissions. Would you do so, briefly, having regard to the clock?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Having heard what's been said, what do you invite us to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May it please the Court, what we would invite the Court to do in these circumstances, which unfortunately are very close to circumstances that the Court will see in the papers of some time ago, is to identify, well, number 1, that a further order be issued directing the Federation to, in fact, comply with the order -- make further efforts to comply and to, in fact, comply with the outstanding order in the following respects. We suggest that this order, as this matter has now been languishing since early February of this year and, as the Court knows, we are in trial on this matter and the information is essential, that there be a further response in 10 days from the date of the Court's order. That the Court direct the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina to identify specific senior officials, probably at the minister level, who are specifically responsible for complying with the Court's order. It appears, and I don't feel terribly strongly about this, but it appears from the information to date that the most likely responsible officials are the Minister of Defence and the Minister of Justice, I would say primarily the former, but because Ministries of Justice tend to deal with legal and other matters reflecting of governments, I think it would be appropriate as well. That in addition these officials be named both by -- well, by the Court and specifically also by the government. That is, the Court, I believe based on the law that I've reviewed, Your Honours, in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal, this Court has the authority to issue an order to the government to identify these people and, secondly, to direct these people to comply with the Court's order. And, further, that this will put the case in the position where, in the unfortunate event that compliance is not forthcoming, it will give the Court maximum leeway to direct further consequences or sanction upon identified individuals as opposed to an anonymous government organisation. So that's what we essentially asked for, Your Honour. As I understand it, again, the government itself, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, needs to direct to these identified individuals that it is their responsibility, on behalf of that government, to comply with the Court's order and that not to comply would not only violate their own government's orders but obviously ultimately this Court's orders, which then would expose them, in our view, ultimately to sanctions under Rule 77. That's what we would seek, Your Honour. Mr. Nice has asked me -- Your Honour, he has re-entered the room. Could I consult with him for a moment if he has additional --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I think we probably need to know where our authority is for issuing an order to specific individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I think that, Your Honour, and I don't have it in front of me, I'm happy to submit any briefs the Court would find helpful, but I think the authority can likely be found in the Appeals Chamber decision in the Blaskic subpoena litigation. I don't think there's authority in the first instance for the Court to subpoena a specific government official, but it's my understanding from that litigation that the Tribunal, the Trial Chamber, has the authority to direct the government, to whom it can issue orders, to identify responsible persons who either have knowledge of the archive or who can be directed to obtain and report knowledge on the archive. The government can be ordered to identify those people, who can then be identified to the Court. That government can order those individuals to comply with the Court's order. If they fail to do so, it's my understanding, they then become subject to further direct inquiry from this Court, because at that point they will not only have violated -- well, they will have violated their own government's order, which I think under the logic of the Tribunal's jurisprudence, means that they then become subject to further consequences from this Chamber. I think some of this may be under Rule 77, but specifically in terms of binding orders, I think most of this is laid out in the Blaskic appeals decision. But I'm certainly happy, Your Honour, to file any briefs that the Court may find helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour, Mr. Nice has reminded me that if, in fact, part of the answer is that some document -- either the documents exist, in somebody's view, or that some exist and some don't, again I think the Court would agree with us, we need to have some position -- that needs to be stated to this Court in such a fashion that there are some consequences that can be visited upon that person or persons if they provide this Court with false, deceptive, or incomplete information. With all respect to Mr. Tomic, a respective coming in and making a narrative account to the Court, who is not under oath, it is not a certification, it doesn't get us very far. Anyone can come in, and no disrespect to counsel, but anyone can come in and give a narrative account to the Court, but it doesn't really ultimately get us anywhere. So as part of the outlined relief that we've requested, Your Honour, if, in fact, part of their response is going to be, "We think this happened on such and such a date," or, "The archive once were here, but we now understand they've been destroyed or they've been taken to someplace else," that has to be done in such a way that it's a certification or a sworn statement, we believe, to the Court, which the Court can then have, if necessary, the most serious leverage on it, if you will, in case this Court is misdirected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'm concerned about -- I'm sorry that I have to leave, but as you know, I've been sorting out this afternoon's matter and I was hoping we might find more time, but I think not. What I was concerned about in hearing Mr. Tomic's account, which was semi-narrative, is that perhaps by questions of him from the Bench, were you to decide this was appropriate, the Court could flesh out that narrative account and find out what it's based on and, in that way, chase down the source that we want to tell us what's actually happened to these documents, because there was quite a lot of -- a number of his answers were semi-specific and yet they weren't attributed in any way. But he must be able to attribute them, and he's before you today. I wondered if it was worth pursuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ahmic, I will invite you -- Mr. Ahmic first, please. You've heard what the Prosecution is suggesting. Is there anything you want to say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, I have nothing to add. I agree with the proposal of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tomic, you've heard what the Prosecutor says, that he suggests that in the light of your replies to us earlier, you must be in a position to assist the Court in finding these documents. Are you in this position?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, I'm afraid my learned friend from the Prosecution overestimates me. I'm not sure, from the position I hold at present, that I can have any substantive influence in that direction. I shall certainly inform the competent persons in the Federation in detail about the seriousness of the matter. But whether I could, for instance, make a statement under oath, I could not say, because under the legal system with which I acted as a defence attorney for years, the institution of oaths was applied to quite different cases, and I must admit that the institution of the taking of an oath in this case is not quite clear to me. What is clear is that anyone speaking in court must do so on the basis of his conscience and honesty, and there is no doubt about that. But I think that colleague Ahmic will agree with me that according to our legal system, the institution of an oath was applied in quite different cases and only exceptionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The point, Mr. Tomic, is this: Do you know where these documents might be?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) No, Your Honour, at this point in time. May I add, if I say that I don't know where they are, this does not mean to say that I mean that they exist, so I should like to express my reservations in that regard. My answer is I do not know where they are at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tomic. We will --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) With your leave, may I make a technical remark?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The representative of the Prosecution proposed that the request be addressed to the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think it would be better to address it to the government of the Federation, because according to the new constitution after Dayton, there is no government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is the government of the Federation and the government of Republika Srpska. So I wouldn't like to resort to using these technical errors, because very often even those of us living in Bosnia-Herzegovina are not fully aware of the details, and I'm saying this in good faith. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will consider these matters and, in due course, let you have our decision. That brings us to the second application which is before us. Now, Mr. Ahmic, did you want to ask for a hearing in closed session about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, Your Honour. I made such a request, but I have been informed by the Registrar that the session is open, and I now agree that it should be an open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, Your Honour, I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. This is an application by the Prosecutor, dated the 16th of April, for documents. We have to apply the criteria which are laid down in the Blaskic appeal decision the 29th of October of 1997; i.e., that the documents are specified as far as reasonably possible, that the documents are relevant to issues in the trial, that the production is not unduly onerous, and that reasonable time is afforded for production. The application, I see, is for a binding order to the Federation to produce documents annexed within 45 calendar days. Is there anything which the Prosecution wish to add to their written pleading in this matter, which appears to set the case out very fully?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Only one, Your Honour. That is that in light of a response received from another government recently, and it's under seal, Your Honour, but it relates to a matter that the Court will be taking up tomorrow, we would seek -- I think maybe if I say it this way, it will become evident. We would seek to add two paragraphs. We would make an oral motion, Your Honour, to add two paragraphs to the annex, which would become annex 42 and 43, and if those could be provided, if not already distributed. One of the stacks I put out this morning was, I think, I hope, was an annex. Did you distribute those? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, I don't know to what you're referring.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Sorry. The annex to our application, which was previously numbered paragraphs 1 through 41. I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This one. Here we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In light of recent developments, which if the Court cares to, we can go into in ex parte session because the matter is under seal by another government, we would seek to add simply paragraphs 42 and 43, which are new. We would not add anything further or comment further on our application, save for the Court's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, who wants to deal with this first, Mr. Ahmic or Mr. Tomic? Well, I invite one of you to start off with your objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) If I understood you correctly, Your Honour, you're asking my objections regarding the annex. I didn't quite catch the full translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm asking for your submissions in relation to the application by the Prosecution for this order in relation to the production of documents. Of course, if you want to say anything about the additional matters which are asked for in the annex, we will hear your submissions on that. But we would like your submissions generally on the application by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I was a little hasty a moment ago, and I apologise for that now. When I mentioned that I had objections regarding the request itself, I was thinking of the annex rather than the order of the Trial Chamber, so I owe you an apology. I have nothing in particular to add to what I have already said. I think that the request is onerous because it requests all documents, recordings, letters, so it imposes maximum demands. I would have certain objections of a minor nature. I see that the position of the persons from whom these documents are required is not even mentioned as a courtesy, and I feel that the high level of this International Tribunal requires a minimum of courtesy. If we do not wish to indicate "XY", the president of such and such a state, but we merely say "Franjo Tudjman", as an attorney I could say we don't know the father's name, we don't know who you mean. There are 15 citizens with the same first and last name. Therefore, in strictly formal terms, the identification is not adequate. I do not insist on this objection, but it is illustrative of a certain position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, it is well that you don't insist on that objection, because there can be nothing in it. Now, if you have serious objections, point them out, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Regarding the definitions given by the counsel for the Prosecution, it is my submission that it would be useful for the Trial Chamber to bear in mind that my position is that the expression -- the "Bosnian Croat forces" is a pluralism, it is redundant and unnecessary, because on the previous page the Prosecutor has correctly explained what the HVO is, and that expression is quite sufficient. That term is quite sufficient to explain what the Croatian forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina are. I think that the Prosecutor has skilfully introduced this term merely in order to be able to introduce other expressions such as "the Bosnian government forces." We feel that this expression is not adequate, not appropriate, and it does not contribute to a proper understanding of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. With all due respect for the President of the Trial Chamber, let me quote a great Englishman, Bertram Russell. "If you say 'nephew', then the uncle is somewhere close by. If you say 'government forces', then the government is nearby." The Prosecutor, interestingly enough, does not define the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. May I add, in passing, that the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina never existed in the formal legal sense. It is a shame that the Prosecutor does not request the official gazettes of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I shall take the liberty of providing Your Honours with some relevant decisions. Therefore, there never existed the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Why is this important? Because the premise of the Prosecution is based on a conventional State, with a government, with an army, with a general staff, with the armed forces. If you review the decision of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated the 20th of June, 1992, on the proclamation of a state of war, you will see that even the government is not mentioned in that decision. Why is it not mentioned? With the President's permission, may I continue this analysis? When you say "the government", you have to take the next step and assess that government on the basis of four criteria; the ability to exercise authority over the whole territory of the country; the question of the population and what is happening to it; three, the ability to implement international treaties. So at that point in time you already had the proclaimed Republika Srpska, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Later on, you had the autonomous province of Western Bosnia, headed by Fikret Abdic, one of the Muslim leaders. So a government, in the conventional sense, does not exist, and therefore "government forces", as a term, is inappropriate. "Muslim forces" would be more appropriate. I do not wish to impose any term, regardless of the fact that in all armies, that is, the HVO, of which I was a volunteer, since my personal name was mentioned, let me say that I opened my own private attorney's office, and as Thomas Mann says, if you are German, you have to suffer the same fate as Germany. As a Croat, I was with my people, with bakers, taxi drivers, and others, and I take pride in that, regardless of the fact that the tendency of this Tribunal to demonise the HVO; therefore --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That was not a proper comment, and you should not be making it. Now, have you got anything further to say, relevant --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- relevant not to a political speech, but to this application? If not, we shall adjourn. Now, is there anything you want to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOMIC
utterances.text: No, no, I do not wish to add anything else. Thank you for hearing me out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll consider this application, too, and give our reasons and order in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Ahmic, you want to say something? I thought you had had -- no, I'm sorry, you didn't have a go. Of course, we will hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) thank you. Mr. Tomic and I are authorised representatives of the Federation at this hearing, so I thought that I should also make my voice heard on this occasion. As one of the authorised representatives of the Federation, I fully support the Prosecutor's request. I think there are no legal obstacles when it comes to the legislation in my country, and I also believe that the legal regulations underlying the International Tribunal also make it quite lawful for such an order, for such a request to be addressed to the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I have no objections whatsoever; I fully endorse the Prosecutor's request. And as for Mr. Tomic's ten-minute-long speech, I think you were quite right in cutting it short, because I do not really think that this is the proper place for it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we make sure, Mr. Ahmic, that we have all the documents which you handed in today? I have one -- perhaps at the end of the hearing you could check with the registry to make sure they have the documents. I have one which I will hand over now to the registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. AHMIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a housekeeping matter --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The same type of housekeeping matter, Your Honour, that the Court was just addressing: If the Court -- just for the purposes of the record, in case there is any possible future consideration or what have you, can I propose -- and really the numbering doesn't -- whatever the registry is happy with is fine with me. I would simply propose offhand that the summary chart, for purposes of identification, be Prosecution 1; that the packet of exhibits be Prosecution 2; and that the confidential report that was tendered only to the Court be Prosecution 3. And again, only for the purposes of having no dispute about what these items were, for the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, we'll adjourn now. We'll sit again to hear the next matter in an hour and a half, 10 past 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 12:40 p.m., sine die. 24 25
